title: Abraham bargains (Genesis 18:16–33)
hook: fifty righteous, forty, thirty, ten: Abraham argues with God for a city

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospitality: an old man running at noon to feed three strangers. Your line was strangers bring god.

At a yard sale, haggling has its own steps. One person names a price. The other laughs and names a lower one. Somebody walks away; somebody calls them back. Somewhere in the middle, a deal. Genesis puts that dance somewhere no one would expect. Yesterday's visitors get up and look toward Sodom, a city the story says is full of wickedness. Abraham walks with them to see them off. The Lord says, in effect, shall I hide from Abraham what I'm about to do? And Abraham, who just served lunch, starts to haggle with God.
screen: `THE STEPS OF A HAGGLE.` → `THE VISITORS LOOK TOWARD SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM HAGGLES WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: First, the opening bid. Abraham steps closer and asks: will you destroy the just with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty just people in the city. Will you spare it for them? Then a line that's almost shocking: shall not the judge of all the earth do what is just? He holds God to God's own justice. And God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Second, the haggling. Abraham keeps going, and he knows how bold he's being. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes." Dust, like the clay of the first human. And still he speaks. Forty-five? Yes. Forty? Yes. Thirty? Yes. Twenty? Yes. Again and again he humbles himself, and asks again. Third, the last number. Let not my Lord be angry, he says, I'll speak only once more. Ten? And God says: "I will not destroy it for the sake of ten." Notice who never says no. God never refuses. It's Abraham who stops asking. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Catechism turns to this scene when it teaches about intercession, prayer on behalf of others: a friend of God standing between a city and its judgment. Catholics pray for others in the same spirit, and at Mass in the prayer of the faithful.
screen: `WILL YOU DESTROY THE JUST?` · `I AM DUST AND ASHES.` · `FIFTY, FORTY, THIRTY, TWENTY, TEN.` · `GOD NEVER SAYS NO.` · then, large: `FOR THE SAKE OF TEN.`

segments.voice: Choose a place that needs mercy, your street, a hospital ward, a prison, a city in the news, a country at war, and picture the good people in it, the ones trying, even if there aren't many. If you pray, ask mercy for it, then ask again, a little more boldly, the way Abraham did; if you don't, simply wish it well, and keep wishing.
Abraham bargains. Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten: an old man asking God, again and again, to spare a city for the sake of the just in it.
Your line: argue for mercy. Even ten just people were worth the asking. That's the week.

howItsDone: At Mass, the prayer of the faithful asks God's help for the Church, the world, people in need and the local community, and Catholics also pray for others by name in their own prayers.

fork.setup: you're Abraham. God has agreed to spare the city for twenty just people. you've already pushed five times. what do you do?
options: thank God and stop at twenty.

fork.reveal: he begs God not to be angry, and asks for ten. God says: "I will not destroy it for the sake of ten."

original.note: Hebrew: righteous, just. Abraham's whole argument turns on the tsaddikim, the just ones in the city.

chat.says: What happened when Abraham tried to bargain with God over Sodom?
options: He asked again and again, down to ten, and God never once said no.
God agreed to fifty, then told him firmly to stop asking for more.
He asked mercy only for his nephew's family, not for the whole city.
chat.meaning: From fifty down to ten, God agrees every time; it's Abraham who stops asking. The Catechism uses this scene to teach intercession.
